blurb: What happens between your phone and the internet on mobile data: masts, SIMs, sharing the airwaves, and what 5G really changed.

lessons.title: From your phone to the internet

steps.p: When you open an app on mobile data, your phone sends radio waves to the nearest mast (a cell tower), usually within a few kilometres.
steps.analogy: Like a walkie-talkie, but one that talks to a tower instead of a friend.

steps.p: The country is divided into many small zones called cells, each served by its own mast. Neighbouring cells use different settings so they don't drown each other out.

visual.caption: Coverage is a patchwork of small zones.

steps.p: The mast only handles the last bit through the air. From there, your data travels through fibre-optic cables — called backhaul — into the operator's network.
The operator's central computers check who you are, keep track of where you are, count your data use, and pass your traffic out to the internet.
Each generation — 2G, 3G, 4G, 5G — is a new set of rules for this journey, roughly every decade, each faster and more efficient.

cards.q: Why is mobile coverage called a "cellular" network?
options: The area is split into many small zones, each served by its own mast
cards.hint: Look at the patchwork in step 2.
cards.why: Small zones called cells. Splitting the map lets the same frequencies be reused in non-neighbouring cells, so millions of phones can share limited airwaves.

cards.statement: When you call someone standing right next to you, your two phones talk to each other directly.
cards.why: False. Both phones talk to the mast, and the call goes through the operator's network — even if you're in the same room.

cards.q: What is "backhaul" in a mobile network?
options: The cables carrying traffic from masts back into the operator's network
Data used by apps in the background
cards.why: The cables behind the mast. The air is only the first hop; the rest of the journey is mostly fibre.

cards.title: A single cell can cover a few hundred metres in a city — or tens of kilometres in open countryside.
cards.detail: Cities use many small cells because more cells means more capacity for crowds. Rural areas use big cells because there are fewer people to share them.

cards.why: True. 1G (1980s) was analogue voice, 2G added texts, 3G brought mobile internet, 4G made video practical, and 5G adds more speed and capacity.

cards.title: How millions of phones share the air

steps.p: Radio frequencies (spectrum) are a limited resource. Governments auction slices to mobile operators for exclusive use, often for billions.
steps.analogy: Like renting lanes on a motorway: each operator gets its own lanes.

steps.p: Low frequencies travel far and get through walls; high frequencies carry more data but fade quickly.
Each mast divides its frequencies into tiny slices of time and frequency, and hands them out to phones thousands of times a second.

steps.h: Your SIM proves who you are
steps.p: The SIM (or eSIM) holds a secret key. The network sends a challenge only the right key can answer — proving you're a paying customer.
As you move, your phone measures nearby masts and the network switches you to a better one, mid-call, without you noticing.
steps.analogy: Like a relay race baton passed between runners while you keep moving.

cards.q: What does a SIM card mainly do?
options: Proves to the network which customer you are
cards.why: Identity. It holds a secret key used to answer the network's challenge, proving you're allowed on and which plan to bill.

cards.q: Why do operators value low frequencies, below about 1 GHz?
options: They travel further and get through walls better
cards.hint: Look at the comparison in step 2.
cards.why: Range and reach. One low-band mast can cover a wide rural area and reach deep inside buildings.

cards.statement: An eSIM still holds a secret key — it's just a chip built into the phone that downloads operator profiles.
cards.why: True. Same security idea, no plastic card. You can switch operator by downloading a new profile.

cards.title: A 2021 US auction of mid-band 5G spectrum raised more than $80 billion.
cards.detail: These frequencies hit a sweet spot of decent range and high capacity. Operators paid that much because spectrum is the scarce raw material of mobile networks.

cards.statement: When you roam abroad, the foreign network checks your identity with your home operator.
cards.why: True. The foreign network asks your home operator to verify your SIM, then bills it for your use.

steps.p: 5G uses new, wider slices of spectrum, especially mid-band around 3.5 GHz, so each mast can carry much more data.
Millimetre-wave 5G uses very high frequencies — extremely fast but with a range of only a couple of hundred metres, blocked by walls or even a hand.
5G masts have dozens of tiny antennas that aim focused beams at individual phones (beamforming), instead of spraying signal everywhere.
steps.analogy: A spotlight instead of a floodlight.

steps.p: 5G can cut the wait for a response, which matters for gaming, video calls and, one day, remote machines.
Video is the big user of data. Higher quality uses much more.

cards.q: Millimetre-wave 5G can be extremely fast. What's its big weakness?
options: Very short range, easily blocked by walls, trees or even a hand
It uses lots of battery in other phones
cards.why: Short range. Very high frequencies carry huge amounts of data but fade fast, so they're used in busy spots like stadiums.

cards.q: Roughly how much mobile data does an hour of HD video use?
cards.why: About 1–3 GB. That's why streaming on mobile data eats through a plan fast.

cards.statement: Seeing a 5G icon guarantees your connection is faster than 4G.
cards.why: False. Some 5G runs on low frequencies with modest speeds, and a crowded or distant mast can be slow whatever the icon says.

cards.title: The first text message, sent in December 1992, simply said "Merry Christmas".
cards.detail: It was typed on a computer and sent to a phone on the UK's Vodafone network. Texts squeezed into spare capacity on 2G's control channels.

cards.statement: Beamforming means a mast aims focused signal toward individual phones.
cards.why: True. Many small antennas time their signals so they add up in your direction, boosting speed and reducing interference.

steps.p: Everyone near a mast shares its capacity. At a concert or football match, speeds collapse even with full bars.
steps.analogy: Like a motorway: the road's the same, but rush hour makes everyone slow.

steps.p: Signal bars show how strong the radio link is — not how busy the mast is or how fast the network behind it is.
With a weak signal, your phone transmits harder and retries more, which uses noticeably more battery.
Mobile signals are "non-ionising": each tiny packet of energy is far too weak to break chemical bonds or damage DNA, unlike X-rays or ultraviolet light.
Video quality and autoplay are the biggest levers. Downloading on WiFi helps too.

cards.statement: The number of signal bars tells you how fast your mobile data will be.
cards.why: False. Bars show signal strength. A crowded mast or busy network can be slow even at full bars.

cards.q: Why can't 5G radio waves damage DNA the way X-rays can?
options: They're non-ionising: each packet of energy is far too weak to break chemical bonds
cards.hint: Look at the scale in step 4.
cards.why: Too little energy per packet. Damage to DNA needs energy above a threshold. Radio waves are far below it, however many there are.

cards.title: A typical phone transmits at about a fifth of a watt at most — far less than a small light bulb.
cards.detail: And it usually uses much less: the network tells each phone to turn its power down when close to a mast, saving battery and reducing interference.

cards.q: Your plan runs out mid-month. Which change usually saves the most data?
options: Lowering video quality and turning off autoplay
cards.why: Video settings. Video is by far the biggest user of mobile data; texts and web pages are tiny by comparison.

cards.q: At a packed stadium you have full bars but data barely works. Why?
options: Thousands of people are sharing the same mast's capacity
Full bars mean the mast is off
cards.why: Shared capacity. The signal is strong, but the mast's capacity is split among thousands of phones.

cards.title: Find your data-hungry apps
cards.body: Your phone tracks mobile data use per app. One or two apps usually account for most of it.
cards.challenge: Open your phone's mobile data settings and find your top three apps. Turn off mobile data for any that don't need it.
